opus-5.5.text:
I think a big part of it was timing and simplicity. When I started working on Tianshou back at Tsinghua, a lot of the existing RL libraries were either really heavy, hard to read, or tied to older frameworks like TensorFlow 1. If you wanted to modify an algorithm for your own research, you often had to dig through layers and layers of abstraction. So one of the main goals was to make it clean and modular, written in pure PyTorch, so that a researcher could actually read the code and understand what's going on.

Another thing was performance. We put a lot of effort into the data pipeline, things like the replay buffer design and vectorized environments, so that training was actually fast, not just elegant on paper. When people benchmarked it and saw it could train something like CartPole or Atari agents quickly, that helped a lot with adoption.

And I'd say we also cared about engineering quality more than a typical research codebase does: unit tests, documentation, type hints, consistent APIs across algorithms. In academia, many people write code just to get the paper out, and then nobody maintains it. We tried to treat it like a real software project. I think users can feel that difference. When something works reliably and the docs answer your questions, you stick with it and you recommend it to others.

So I'd say it's a combination: a clean design, good speed, and taking the engineering side seriously. Honestly, a bit of luck too, being at the right time when PyTorch was taking over and people were looking for an RL library that fit that ecosystem.

r001.rationale: The response describes Tianshou as clean and modular, but does not say that adding a desired feature required code changes in only one location.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think a big part of it was timing and frustration. When I started Tianshou, it was around 2018, 2019, and most of the RL codebases out there were either huge research monoliths or one-off scripts someone wrote for a paper. If you wanted to try a new idea, you'd spend days just untangling the code before you could change anything.

So the first thing I cared about was keeping it small and readable. I wanted the core to be something a student could read in an afternoon and actually understand. That meant a clean separation between the pieces: the environment wrapper, the replay buffer, the collector that gathers data, the policy, and the trainer that ties it all together. Once those boundaries were clear, adding a new algorithm became maybe a hundred or two hundred lines instead of rewriting half the project.

The second thing was that we were pure PyTorch from the start. A lot of popular frameworks at the time were TensorFlow-based, and the research community was clearly moving to PyTorch, so we caught that wave. People could read our DQN or PPO implementation and it looked like the pseudocode in the paper, which matters a lot when you're trying to learn or debug.

Third, speed. We put real effort into the vectorized environments and the batch data structure, so you could run many environments in parallel and the data pipeline wouldn't be the bottleneck. We also made sure the results matched the published numbers on standard benchmarks. That reproducibility bought a lot of trust, because people had been burned before by implementations that silently underperformed.

And then there's the community side. We had good documentation and tutorials early, and we were responsive on GitHub. A lot of contributors came in with a fix or a new algorithm, and we tried to make that easy. Over time it kind of snowballed. I'd also say the Chinese research community picked it up quickly, partly because of the Tsinghua connection, and that gave it a strong base to grow from.

If I had to summarize, I'd say it's a framework that respects the user's time. It doesn't hide things from you, it doesn't make you fight it, and it works out of the box. That turns out to be rarer than it should be.

r001.rationale: The response says the clear component boundaries made adding an algorithm require only about 100–200 lines, but it does not state that changes for a desired feature were confined to a single location.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s because Tianshou makes it easier to go from understanding a reinforcement learning algorithm to actually experimenting with it. We tried to keep the code readable and the interfaces flexible, so users could start with an existing implementation and then modify it for their own research without having to understand the entire framework first.

There’s also a lot of engineering around reinforcement learning that isn’t the algorithm itself—collecting data, managing replay buffers, evaluating policies. Having reusable components for those tasks lets people focus on their ideas. And I think the community matters a lot: people trying it, reporting problems, and contributing improvements make the framework more useful over time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a big part of it is the balance between ease of use and flexibility. In reinforcement learning, you want to get a baseline running quickly, but you also need to understand the implementation and change things for your own research. Tianshou tries to make both possible through a modular design.

Reliability matters, too. Having an algorithm implemented is one thing; making it work consistently is another. And I think the community is a big part of the appeal—people asking questions, reporting issues, and contributing improvements make the framework more useful over time.
